segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Few movements in cinema have been as influential as the French New Wave, or nouvelle vague. What began as a gathering of ambitious young critics working at a film magazine turned into a group of filmmakers whose work redefined modern cinema.
segments.text: Few movements in cinema have been as influential as the French New Wave, or nouvelle vague. What began as a gathering of ambitious young critics working at a film magazine turned into a group of filmmakers whose work redefined modern cinema.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The movement's origins lie in the strong presence of two individuals: film archivist Henri Langlois and critic André Bazin. The latter was one of the founders, in 1950, of the magazine Cahiers du cinéma; Langlois was a co-founder of the Cinémathèque Française, a film archive that held regular screenings in Paris.

The latter was one of the founders, in nineteen fifty, of the magazine Cahiers du cinéma; Langlois was a co-founder of the Cinémathèque Française, a film archive that held regular screenings in Paris.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Many of the future members of the French New Wave knew Langlois personally and attended the Cinémathèque with almost religious fervor, often discussing the films they had seen into the early hours. Among the filmmakers who later wrote for Cahiers du cinéma were François Truffaut (1932-1984), Jean-Luc Godard (b. 1930), Jacques Rivette (b. 1928), and Eric Rohmer (1920-2010).

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The magazine scorned the conservative French cinema of the time and instead championed American directors and the development of an auteur theory. A director's recognizable signature - a personal stamp that defined a filmmaker's work - was seen as a sign of greatness. The Cahiers critics joined other regulars of the Cinémathèque in their desire to make their own films.

tracks.title: Learn more: Characteristics of French New Wave cinema

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Emphasis on "auteur cinema": this "new wave" brought many innovations. The artists were interested in making auteur-driven cinema, in which the screenplay and the direction were truly valued, as was the acting. It was in this context that the expression "auteur cinema" was coined. Breaking narrative linearity: One of the elements the French New Wave subverts is linearity. There was no concern with telling the story in the chronological order of events, which led to a rupture in narrative structure. Emphasis on outdoor settings: Outdoor locations were also widely used. Natural light and everyday settings came to be valued, unlike what had been done until then, when scenes were shot in studios and controlled spaces. The filmmakers wanted to show the pulsing life of the streets, passersby, and everyday life as the backdrop for their stories. Everyday themes: The themes addressed raised common questions, day-to-day hardships, and mundane reflections on life. Because of this, acting was very important, with improvisation and spontaneity even being emphasized. In addition, other subjects such as romantic and sexual freedom and postwar pacification also appear frequently. Innovation in filmmaking: On the technical side, the French New Wave experimented with new framings and camera movements, and also innovated in the editing of scenes.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Though immature, the early films of Godard, Rivette, and Rohmer marked an aesthetic shift, moving the action from studios to real locations. This was made possible by technological advances, as cheaper high-quality portable cameras and faster film stocks were by then available, allowing access to almost any place and shooting without the aid of lighting.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The French New Wave officially began with Le Beau Serge (1958), directed by Claude Chabrol (1930-2010), but it was Truffaut's The 400 Blows (1959) and Godard's Breathless (1960) that made the biggest waves. After being banned from the Cannes Film Festival in 1958 for his criticism of French cinema, Truffaut triumphed at the festival the following year. Partly autobiographical and shot in the neighborhood where the filmmaker grew up, The 400 Blows stars Jean-Pierre Léaud as Antoine Doinel, a character whose life and loves the director would chronicle in five films over the next 20 years.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: At once good-humored, playful, daring, and insolent, Breathless came to be seen as the film that defined the French New Wave. It was based on a story by Truffaut and displayed all the elements that underpinned the movement's style. Godard mixed cinematic and literary references, even going so far as to cast Jean-Pierre Melville (1917-1973) - one of the French directors Cahiers du cinéma admired - as a character in the film.

tracks.title: Vivre sa vie: film en douze tableaux

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: According to some sources, it was Melville who suggested that Godard cut the film so that scenes jumped straight into the action, creating the jump cut that disrupted the flow of conventional "invisible" editing. The story itself was disposable, as alluded to by a character in Godard's third film, Vivre sa vie: film en douze tableaux (1962), who says of a book she is reading: "the story is silly, but the book is very well written."

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Le Signe du lion (Sign of the Lion, 1962), by Eric Rohmer (1920-2010), was received with less enthusiasm, but its shooting locations and literary references place it in the same group as his colleagues' films. Paris nous appartient (Paris Belongs to Us, 1961), by Jacques Rivette (1928-2016), was the longest of the early New Wave films, but the way it explores Paris makes it one of the most beautiful, even if it lacks the bold sloppiness of Godard's and Truffaut's films.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Claude Chabrol, probably more than any other director of the French New Wave, was always fascinated by a single genre, and he found in it a gold mine for exploring human weakness. After his debut feature, Le Beau Serge, a simple portrait of French provincial life, The Cousins (1959) served as the model for the films that followed it. That same year, À double tour (Web of Passion, 1959) successfully recombined the movement's elements within a more classical narrative. Chabrol kept going down this path, building a distinctive body of work.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Alain Resnais (b. 1922) is another director whose early works align with the French New Wave. Last Year at Marienbad (1961) is arguably his most enigmatic film. The screenplay was written by Alain Robbe-Grillet (1922-2008), a member of an avant-garde literary movement - the nouveau roman - whose creative process became intertwined with that of the French New Wave.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Truffaut's Jules and Jim (1962) became one of the emblematic films of the French New Wave. The film, which tells of a love triangle set before, during, and after World War I, uses several techniques and elements that became trademarks of the new style, such as the incorporation of newsreel footage, freeze frames, dolly shots, and voice-over narration.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Godard was the most prolific filmmaker of the movement and kept experimenting with genre, showing his love of literature, cinema, and philosophy in films such as A Woman Is a Woman (1961) and Band of Outsiders (1964). Godard's films, like so many others of the French New Wave, are full of references to American cinema - the unscrupulous characters of Breathless and Band of Outsiders (1964) are ardent fans of Hollywood B movies.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Godard went on to influence generations of younger filmmakers. When Quentin Tarantino (b. 1963) named his production company A Band Apart, he was paying homage to the legendary French director. Pierrot le Fou (1965) would mark the start of the overt politicization of Godard's work, which only grew over the course of the decade.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Later, the close-knit confrérie of the French New Wave would be torn apart by infighting and quarrels. By the end of the 1960s, Truffaut and Godard were barely speaking. But at the start of the movement, the members of the group generally collaborated and helped one another. The group did not consist only of directors. Among the actors strongly associated with the French New Wave are Jeanne Moreau, Anna Karina, Michel Bouquet, Jean-Paul Belmondo, Jean-Claude Brialy, Stéphane Audran and, of course, Truffaut's cinematic alter ego, Jean-Pierre Léaud. Behind the cameras was another group of frequent collaborators, such as cinematographers Henri Decaë, Sacha Vierny, Nicolas Hayer, Néstor Almendros, and Raoul Coutard, editors Lila Herman, Cécile Decugis, Claudine Bouché, and Agnès Guillemot, and composers Georges Delerue and Michel Legrand.
